lessons.title: Everyday reductions
lessons.explain: Reductions help you understand fast speech and sound relaxed in conversation.
lessons.caution: These are informal spoken forms. Do not write them in essays, emails or formal exams, and avoid them in a formal presentation.

lessons.title: kinda, sorta, lemme, gimme
lessons.explain: More casual reductions you will hear constantly in films and real conversation.
lessons.caution: Informal only. In an IELTS or job interview, keep the full forms.

lessons.title: hafta, needa, useta
lessons.explain: More obligation and habit reductions common in relaxed spoken English.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken forms only — never write them.

items.text: She has to finish it today.

lessons.title: coulda, woulda, shoulda
lessons.explain: Past modal reductions — very common when talking about regrets or hypothetical situations.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'could have' in full in formal writing.

lessons.title: dunno, dontcha, whatcha
lessons.explain: Very casual reductions common in songs, films and relaxed conversation among friends.
lessons.caution: Very informal — only with close friends, never in professional or exam contexts.

lessons.title: outta, offa, cuppa
lessons.explain: Common preposition-linked reductions in casual speech.
lessons.caution: Informal only.

items.text: Take it off of the table.

lessons.title: c'mon, gonna be, s'more
lessons.explain: Everyday exclamations and casual phrases with heavy reduction.
lessons.caution: Informal only.

lessons.title: Reductions in casual questions
lessons.explain: Question-starters reduce heavily in fast, casual conversation.
lessons.caution: Only for casual, spoken contexts.

lessons.title: Reductions with numbers and time
lessons.explain: Casual speech often reduces time phrases too.
points: in a minute → in a min
lessons.caution: Fine in casual talk, not in writing.

items.text: Give me a couple of minutes.
I'll be there in a minute.
items.pattern: I'll be there in a min.

lessons.title: probably, trying to, supposed to
lessons.explain: More common casual reductions heard constantly in relaxed conversation.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: let's, gimme that, y'all
lessons.explain: Casual reductions common among friends and in American informal speech.
points: give it to me → gimme that
lessons.caution: Very informal — 'y'all' is regional (Southern US) but widely understood.

lessons.title: Casual numbers in fast speech
lessons.explain: Round numbers reduce their middle consonant sounds in fast, casual American speech.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — always say the full form in formal contexts.

items.text: About a hundred people showed up.
items.pattern: About a hunnerd people showed up.

lessons.title: Words that shrink one syllable in casual talk
lessons.explain: A different set of everyday words that regularly lose a syllable in fast, relaxed speech.
lessons.caution: Fine in casual speech; say the full form clearly in formal presentations.

items.text: We need a general idea first.
items.pattern: We need a gen'ral idea first.

lessons.title: I'ma and other ultra-casual forms
lessons.explain: Very informal reductions you'll hear in songs and casual American speech, but should never use in professional settings.
lessons.caution: Extremely informal — friends/song lyrics only, never professional contexts.

lessons.title: More casual greeting reductions
lessons.explain: Extra everyday greeting reductions beyond what's up / how's it going.
points: how are you → how ya doin'
good to see you → good to see ya
lessons.caution: Casual spoken forms only.

lessons.title: oughta, don't hafta, wantcha
lessons.explain: More obligation and desire reductions common in relaxed American speech.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: You don't hafta come if you don't want to.
items.pattern: You don't hafta come if you don't want to.

lessons.title: Famous extreme reduction: 'Did you eat yet?'
lessons.explain: This is a classic example of how far casual American reduction can go — several words blur into what sounds like one.
lessons.caution: Extremely informal — for recognizing fast native speech, not for your own formal speaking.

lessons.title: 'because of' and 'sort of a'
lessons.explain: Two more common phrase-level reductions in casual conversation.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: It's sort of a weird situation.

lessons.title: Casual yes/no: yep, nope, uh-huh
lessons.explain: Very common casual alternatives to 'yes' and 'no' in relaxed spoken English.
lessons.caution: Casual conversation only — use 'yes'/'no' in formal or exam contexts.

lessons.title: 'want a' (thing) vs 'want to' (action)
lessons.explain: Both reduce to a similar-sounding 'wanna', but one is followed by a noun and the other by a verb — worth noticing the difference.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: wouldn't have → wouldn'ta
lessons.explain: The negative version of 'would have' reduces the same way as the positive form.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'wouldn't have' in full otherwise.

lessons.title: just 'cause, gonna need
lessons.explain: Two more everyday reductions common in casual explanations and requests.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: I did it just 'cause I wanted to.
items.pattern: I did it just 'cause I wanted to.

lessons.title: ain't — am not, is not, are not
lessons.explain: 'Ain't' replaces am not/is not/are not/has not/have not in very casual speech and is heard everywhere in songs and informal talk.
lessons.caution: Never use in writing or formal speech — considered non-standard grammar, even though extremely common informally.

lessons.title: gotcha — got you
lessons.explain: A very common casual way to say 'I understand' or literally 'caught you'.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — say 'I understand' or 'got it' in professional contexts.

items.text: Got you — I'll send it by five.
items.pattern: Gotcha — I'll send it by five.

items.text: I got you! You looked so surprised.

lessons.title: musta, mighta — must have, might have
lessons.explain: Modal-perfect reductions used for guesses about the past, alongside coulda/woulda/shoulda.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'must have'/'might have' in full otherwise.

lessons.title: shouldn'ta, couldn'ta — negative past modals
lessons.explain: The negative counterparts of coulda/woulda/shoulda, common when talking about regrets.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'shouldn't have'/'couldn't have' in full in formal contexts.

lessons.title: g-dropping: doin', goin', talkin'
lessons.explain: In relaxed speech, the final -ing sound often drops its 'g', so it sounds like -in'. This happens across almost any -ing verb.
lessons.caution: Casual speech only — pronounce the full '-ing' clearly in presentations, interviews and exams.

lessons.title: somethin', nothin', anythin'
lessons.explain: The same g-dropping pattern applies to indefinite pronouns ending in -thing.
lessons.caution: Casual speech only.

lessons.title: 'em — them
lessons.explain: 'Them' reduces to 'em (the 'th' drops) after a verb, in very common casual speech.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — say 'them' in full in writing or formal speech.

items.text: Go get them from the car.

lessons.title: 'n' — and
lessons.explain: 'And' reduces to a quick 'n' sound between two closely linked words, especially in set phrases.
lessons.caution: Common in set phrases and fast speech — say 'and' clearly in formal writing.

items.text: We went back and forth about it.
items.pattern: We went back 'n' forth about it.

lessons.title: standalone 'cause — because
lessons.explain: 'Because' on its own (not just 'because of') often shortens to 'cause in casual answers.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'because' in full otherwise.

items.text: I'm tired because I didn't sleep well.
items.pattern: I'm tired 'cause I didn't sleep well.

lessons.title: 'course — of course
lessons.explain: 'Of course' often drops its first word in quick, casual replies.
lessons.caution: Casual spoken only.

lessons.title: aight — all right
lessons.explain: A very common casual pronunciation of 'all right', used to agree or acknowledge.
lessons.caution: Very informal — say 'all right' or 'okay' in professional contexts.

lessons.title: letcha — let you
lessons.explain: 'Let you' reduces the same way 'want you'/'wantcha' does.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: jever — did you ever
lessons.explain: Another extreme fast-speech blend, similar to 'jeetyet' — several words compress into one sound.
lessons.caution: For recognising fast native speech, not for your own formal speaking.

lessons.title: gonna hafta — going to have to
lessons.explain: Two reductions stack together when 'going to' and 'have to' appear side by side.
points: going to have to → gonna hafta
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'going to have to' in full otherwise.

items.text: We're going to have to leave soon.
I'm going to have to call you back.
items.pattern: I'm gonna hafta call you back.

lessons.title: not gonna, wasn't gonna
lessons.explain: The 'gonna' reduction still applies with negatives and past tense.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: innit — isn't it (British)
lessons.explain: A very common British English tag question reduction, used to confirm or add emphasis.
lessons.caution: Very informal British slang — don't use in formal speech, even in the UK.

lessons.title: whaddya say — what do you say
lessons.explain: A casual way to propose something or ask for agreement.
points: what do you say → whaddya say
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: What do you say we grab lunch?

lessons.title: y'know — you know (filler)
lessons.explain: An extremely common filler phrase in casual spoken English, used while thinking or for emphasis.
lessons.caution: Casual filler only — overusing it sounds unpolished even informally.

items.text: It was, you know, kind of awkward.

lessons.title: s'up — what's up
lessons.explain: A very casual greeting, shortened from 'what's up'.
lessons.caution: Very informal greeting between friends only.

lessons.title: tell 'im, ask 'er — him, her
lessons.explain: 'Him' and 'her' also weaken in casual speech, similar to 'them' → 'em.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: kinda sorta — combined hedge
lessons.explain: 'Kinda' and 'sorta' are often combined for extra hedging in very casual speech.
points: kind of sort of → kinda sorta
lessons.caution: Very informal — avoid in any professional or exam context.

items.text: It's kind of, sort of, complicated.

lessons.title: dincha — didn't you
lessons.explain: Another fast-speech question-starter blend, alongside dja and wouldja.
lessons.caution: For recognising fast native speech, not for your own formal speaking.

lessons.title: hadta — had to
lessons.explain: The past-tense form of 'have to' reduces the same way the present form does.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

lessons.title: willcha — will you
lessons.explain: A casual reduction used in informal requests, alongside wouldja and couldja-style forms.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: Will you help me with this?

lessons.title: lotsa, buncha — lots of, bunch of
lessons.explain: Quantity phrases with 'of' reduce the same way 'cup of' does in 'cuppa'.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only.

items.text: I have a bunch of questions.

lessons.title: helluva — hell of a
lessons.explain: A strong informal intensifier meaning 'a very impressive/big'.
lessons.caution: Mildly crude — fine with friends, avoid in professional or polite settings.

items.text: That was a hell of a game.

lessons.title: howdy — how do you do
lessons.explain: A historical reduction of the old greeting 'how do you do', now its own casual, friendly greeting (especially in the Southern US).
lessons.caution: Casual, friendly greeting only.

lessons.title: s'pose — I suppose
lessons.explain: 'I suppose' commonly drops its middle syllable in casual speech, used to express mild uncertainty or reluctant agreement — distinct from 'supposed to' → s'posed to.
lessons.caution: Informal spoken only — write 'I suppose' in full otherwise.
